c1.story:
Ask ten Indians what their biggest financial decision was, and most will say buying a home. Ask ten investors what a real estate stock is, and you will get four different answers, because this industry label covers four very different businesses.

The first is the luxury and premium developer. DLF selling apartments in Gurugram that cost more than most people earn in a lifetime, Lodha and Oberoi doing the same in Mumbai, Godrej Properties running a national brand on land it often shares with landowners. They sell flats off the drawing board, collect money in instalments as the tower rises, and book profit only when they hand over the keys, years later. Their best weapon is land bought cheap, sometimes decades ago, which turns into extraordinary margins when prices rise.

The second is the regional developer: Prestige, Brigade and Sobha, who grew up in Bengaluru, and Aditya Birla Real Estate building out the old Century Textiles land. They sell more, smaller flats, often to salaried professionals with home loans, and they know their cities street by street. Their margins are thinner, but their volumes are steadier.

The third does not sell at all. Phoenix Mills builds malls and keeps them, collecting rent plus a share of each shop's sales, year after year. Anant Raj is turning land around Delhi into data centres and offices. These are annuity businesses, valued more like a growing bond than a cyclical trade.

And the fourth door is an accident of classification: toll-road trusts like the NHAI's own InvIT, and a state housing and infrastructure lender, HUDCO, filed in this industry but not developers at all.

A developer sells you a promise. An annuity owner sells you a lease. The market prices them very differently, and it should.

Why does it matter? Because a strong pre-sales quarter is big news for the first two doors and irrelevant for the third, while a rise in bond yields hurts the third and fourth and barely touches a luxury developer whose buyers pay from their stock-market gains.
c1.read:
Four tiles, one per door. Read each top to bottom.

  • The name and line under it describe how the money comes in: off-plan flat sales in instalments with profit on handover, more and smaller flats in home cities on shared land, rent from malls and offices that rises every few years, and toll cash or lending income.
  • The tickers are the listed names behind each door; click one for its stock page. The fourth tile is worth a second look: NHIT, CUBEINVIT and VERTIS are road trusts, and HUDCO is a lender. The classification puts them here, but almost nothing else on this page is about them, so treat them separately.
  • The profit bar sits at high for two doors: luxury developers, because land bought cheap and brand pricing leave a fat margin on each flat, and annuity owners, because a filled mall keeps most of its rent. Regional developers sit at medium, with thinner margins on mid-income flats. The road trusts and the lender also sit at medium.
  • The last line is your bet. Read the luxury blurb carefully: it is a bet on rich buyers and on land bought cheap. Both halves matter. A luxury developer that bought its land at the top of the market does not earn the high bar.

Below, the analogy maps the doors onto a tailor, a ready-made shop, the market building and a toll booth, and the so-what line gives the test: residential is a bet on pre-sales and land, annuity on rent and rates. Decide which one you own before reading any results headline, because the two read the same quarter in opposite ways.

c2.story:
Every flat in India begins as a piece of land and a stack of paperwork. The kitchen of this industry has five stations, and the most valuable one is the first.

Station one is land and approvals. A developer can buy land outright, which ties up cash for years. It can sign a joint development with the landowner, who contributes the plot in exchange for a share of the flats or the revenue, which is how Godrej Properties grew so fast with relatively little capital. Or it can pick up land and stalled projects from bankrupt rivals through the insolvency courts. Then comes the queue: environment, fire, height, airport clearance, municipal plans. Land without approvals is dead capital.

Station two is the launch. Plans are approved, the project is registered with the state RERA, and sales open. In a hot market the best projects sell out within days: DLF's Arbour launch in Gurugram in 2023 became the headline example.

Station three is construction, and here listed developers mostly step back. They hire contractors like L&T and Shapoorji Pallonji to pour the concrete over three to five years, paid from an escrowed slice of buyer money. Sobha is the famous exception, building in-house and making many of its own materials.

Station four is sales and collections, which runs in parallel with construction. Flats are sold through brokers and the developer's own team, and buyers pay in stages, mostly funded by home loans from banks and housing finance companies.

Station five is handover, when revenue finally hits the books, and for some developers it is also the start of a rent stream, as malls and offices are leased and kept.

A developer's real factory is the land bank. The cement mixer is rented.

Notice what is missing: any foreign rival. Real estate is the most local business in India, decided city by city and often micro-market by micro-market. A developer who dominates Bengaluru's east can be a nobody in Pune.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, then the band row underneath.

The five boxes follow a project from raw land to handed-over home. Under each station name you see what happens and who stands there. Notice the names: landowners and authorities on the left, the listed developers at launch, hired contractors at construction, listed developers again at sales, and buyers and tenants at the end.

The band row shows who holds each station, and it alternates. The first band is landowners and authorities, the second is coloured Indian listed, the third is contractors, the fourth is Indian listed again, and the fifth is buyers and tenants. The listed developers hold the two stations that touch the customer, the launch and the sale, and outsource the one in between.

That alternation is the so-what line in pictures. Listed developers own the land and the customer and rent the concrete. So their risk is not the price of cement; it is land bought too dear at station one and buyers who stop paying at station four.

There is no second band row, because no foreign rival stands at any station. The note under the bands tells you where the business is: the Mumbai region, Gurugram and Noida, Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad make up most of what listed developers sell, and land and stamp duty are the costs that differ city to city.

Use the diagram to place news. A big land deal is a station one story whose payoff arrives at station two in a year or so. A home-loan rate change lands on station four first. A slow handover year shows up at station five, in reported revenue, years after the sales were made.

c3.story:
Who buys a flat in Gurugram that costs as much as a small company? The answer explains most of this cycle.

Start with the luxury buyer: business owners, senior professionals, founders who have just sold shares in an IPO, promoters who have taken some money off the table. Their down payment comes from the stock market, not a salary. So when the market has a great year, luxury sales follow; when it has a bad one, they stall. Home-loan rates barely enter the calculation. That is why luxury kept selling through 2023 and 2024 even with rates high, and why it led the boom.

Then the non-resident Indian, buying a premium home in the city where they grew up, in Kochi, Hyderabad or Mumbai. They watch the rupee against the dollar and the dirham: a weaker rupee makes an Indian flat cheaper in their own currency. Their incomes follow the Gulf and US job markets.

The salaried IT professional is the engine of Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad. They buy mid and premium flats on home loans, so their decision turns on hiring, pay rises and the EMI. First-time and affordable buyers are more rate-sensitive still, and they are the ones being priced out today, as city prices have outrun salaries.

Luxury runs on the stock market. Affordable runs on the EMI. That is why they moved in opposite directions.

Then the annuity customers. Global capability centres and IT firms lease offices on long terms. Retailers and brands rent mall space and pay a share of their sales. And a newer tile has appeared: cloud and data-centre operators buying powered land and built shells, which is why some land-rich developers near Delhi and Mumbai have discovered a second business.

The last tile, highway users, belongs to the road trusts filed here, and moves with truck freight and the wholesale inflation that sets toll increases.
c3.read:
Eight tiles, each a buyer group, each in three lines: who buys, what they buy and what moves them.

  • The first four, salaried IT professionals, the very rich, NRIs and first-time buyers, are residential buyers. Their drivers differ completely: hiring and EMIs for the first, stock-market wealth and liquidity events for the second, the rupee and foreign jobs for the third, loan rates and subsidies for the fourth. Four kinds of homebuyer, four cycles.
  • The next three, GCCs and IT firms, retailers and brands, and cloud and data-centre operators, are the annuity door's tenants, moved by Western tech budgets, urban spending and AI and cloud capex.
  • The last tile, highway users, belongs to the road trusts in door four.

The useful exercise here is to match each developer to its tiles. A Gurugram luxury developer leans on the very rich and NRIs, so watch the stock market and the rupee. A Bengaluru mid-income developer leans on IT professionals, so watch IT hiring. A mall owner leans on retailers, so watch urban consumption.

Then read the so-what line, the key insight of this card: premium buyers move with stock-market wealth and NRI money, not home-loan rates, which is why luxury held up when affordable housing slumped. It also tells you what would end the luxury run: not a rate rise, but a sharp fall in the stock market.

c4.story:
Here is the strangest fact about a residential developer's accounts: the most important number is not in them.

When a developer launches a tower and sells half the flats in a month, it collects booking amounts and then instalments as the building rises. That value of flats sold, called pre-sales or bookings, is the real top line. But under Indian accounting rules, revenue is recognised only when the flat is completed and handed over, three or four years later. So this year's reported revenue tells you about sales made years ago, and this year's sales will not reach the profit and loss statement until the next cycle may already be turning.

A developer's income statement is a letter from the past. The pre-sales release is the news.

That is why analysts read developers through the cash flow statement and the quarterly operational update instead. How much was sold? How much cash was collected? How much went on construction and land? Is net debt rising or falling? The developers that collapsed in the last downturn, from Unitech to Jaypee, were the ones that borrowed to buy land and then could not sell or deliver.

Look at the shape of the costs too. Land and construction swallow most of each rupee of a flat's price. Selling and marketing take a slice. Interest is often capitalised into inventory, so it hides inside the cost of the flat rather than appearing as a separate line until handover.

The annuity owner's statement looks completely different. A mall or office park costs little in direct inputs; the big lines are people, maintenance and marketing, then depreciation and interest on the loans that built it. Depreciation is large and non-cash, so the cash profit is well above the reported profit. The market values these businesses on rent and cap rates, the yield a buyer would accept for the rent stream, not on earnings per share.

Same industry label, two completely different ways of reading the accounts, and mixing them up is the most common mistake investors make here.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, for a residential developer and for an annuity owner. Read each left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is land and construction. For the residential developer it is the giant: roughly three of every five rupees. For the annuity owner it is tiny, about a twentieth, because the building already exists.
  • The opex bar is selling, marketing and people. The developer spends about an eighth; the annuity owner a little over a quarter, because running a mall means staff, events, upkeep and marketing.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is small for the developer and large for the annuity owner, a little over a quarter, the cost of the buildings and the debt that paid for them.
  • The last bar is what is left: about a fifth for the residential developer, around two-fifths for the annuity owner.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts; hover a bar for the amount. Remember that the residential chart describes flats handed over, which were sold years earlier.

Below the charts, the list of lines tells you what to read. Pre-sales and collections get a yes, even though they are not in the P&L at all. Working capital, interest and net debt also get a yes: land and unfinished flats are the whole balance sheet, and debt is the cycle killer. Revenue and margin get only a sometimes, a rare verdict for a top line, because they describe old sales. Depreciation and capex are sometimes too, mattering for annuity owners more than developers.

c5.story:
Indian real estate runs on long cycles, roughly a decade from boom to bottom, and the last full one is worth knowing in detail because it explains why investors behave as they do today.

The boom ran from 2004 to 2008. Credit was easy, land was bought at almost any price, and developers listed at fat valuations; DLF's IPO in 2007 was the largest Indian listing of its time. Launches sprang up everywhere. The peak dragged on from 2010 to 2012, as prices ran far ahead of incomes and unsold inventory piled up while developers kept launching.

Then came a long, grinding bust from 2013 to 2019, and it rewrote the industry. Projects stalled and buyers waited years for flats they had paid for. Demonetisation in 2016 hit cash transactions. RERA arrived in 2017, forcing developers to register projects, ring-fence buyer money and deliver on time. GST changed the tax structure. Then the IL&FS collapse in 2018 froze the shadow banks that had been funding developers. Many developers went bankrupt, and the homebuyers of Noida became a byword for the cost of trusting the wrong builder.

The bust did not just clear inventory. It cleared out the developers.

The bottom, around 2019 and 2020, was where the next cycle was seeded. Weak developers exited; strong ones picked up land cheap. Covid briefly froze sales, but home-loan rates fell to generational lows, Maharashtra cut stamp duty, and suddenly everyone working from home wanted a bigger flat.

What followed was a boom of a different kind. Buyers burnt by stalled projects went to listed, RERA-compliant developers with brands they trusted. Pre-sales hit records in 2023 and 2024, led by luxury, and the realty index more than doubled. Then, in 2025, unit sales slipped as prices outran salaries, and the stocks fell by a quarter to a third from their peaks even as the RBI cut rates.

Today the arrow points at the peak arc: late up-cycle, prices high, unit sales flattening.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top, labelled with the last full cycle's years: boom from 2004 to 2008, peak from 2010 to 2012, bust from 2013 to 2019 and bottom in 2019 and 2020. Notice that this clock is labelled with an older cycle than most on this site, because real estate cycles are long. The arrow points at the peak arc, labelled late up-cycle, with the detail that prices are high and unit sales are flattening. Hover an arc to read what defined that phase last time, and ask how much of it rhymes today.

The timeline covers the current cycle from 2019: bust at the start, a neutral Covid year, boom through 2024, neutral in 2025 as unit sales slipped, and the latest entry marked as now, describing a plateau.

The four hands are what move the arrow.

  • Unsold inventory in months of sales: rising from lows, marked down. This is the hand that turned first.
  • Listed developers' pre-sales growth: flat to modest. Watch whether growth comes from volume or only from price.
  • Home-loan rates: falling, marked up. The one hand clearly helping.
  • Land deal activity and prices: very active, mixed. Aggressive land buying at high prices is how the next downturn starts.

One hand down, one flat, one up and one mixed: the reading of a cycle at its plateau, still supported by rates but losing momentum in units. The hand to watch most closely is unsold inventory.

c6.story:
The dials that move real estate developers are unusually split, because the industry's buyers are so different. A luxury buyer in south Mumbai and a first-time buyer on the edge of Pune respond to almost opposite forces.

For the mid-income and affordable buyer, the dial is the home-loan rate. A typical buyer borrows most of the flat's price over twenty years or so, so a small change in rate makes a big change in the EMI, and the EMI decides whether the flat is affordable at all. When rates fell to generational lows in 2020, a wave of first-time buyers arrived. When the RBI hiked in 2022 and 2023, that wave thinned. The same dial also sets the developer's own funding cost and, for annuity owners, the value of their rent streams.

For the luxury buyer, the dial is the stock market. A founder who has just sold shares, a promoter who has taken money off the table, a fund manager who has had a good year: they make large down payments from equity gains. That is why luxury boomed while rates were high, and why a sharp fall in the market would hit it first.

To forecast luxury sales, watch the Sensex. To forecast affordable sales, watch the EMI.

IT and services hiring is the third heavy dial, and a neat one, because it works twice: it fills Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad with salaried buyers and fills office parks with tenants at the same time.

Then the supporting cast. Bank credit appetite decides how easily developers get construction finance and buyers get loans. Stamp duty can pull demand forward, as Maharashtra's temporary cut did in 2020, and then leave a hole. Bond yields set the value of rent streams for annuity owners. The rupee and Gulf jobs shape NRI demand. And cement and steel prices matter less than you might think, because developers outsource construction, but they do squeeze margins on flats already sold at a fixed price.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches the business. Notice how many channels run through the buyer's wallet: EMI affordability, down payments from equity, salaries, NRI purchasing power, the upfront cost of stamp duty.
  • A rise does: a green up arrow means a rise helps, a red down arrow means it hurts. Four dials carry red arrows: home-loan and policy rates, cement and steel prices, stamp duty and bond yields. The other six are green. There is no diamond.
  • Weight: three dots sit on three rows: home-loan and policy rates, stock-market wealth and IT and services hiring.

The three three-dot dials map neatly onto the buyer tiles of card three. Rates are the mid-income buyer's dial, the stock market is the luxury buyer's, and IT hiring is the salaried professional's. A developer's exposure to each depends on which buyers it sells to.

The last column shows today's reading where a dial maps to a series we track: the money-market rate, the Nifty, the Nifty IT index, the rupee, a steel series, a bank credit indicator, the FMCG index and a government bond tracker. Stamp duty and Gulf and US jobs show a dash; follow state budgets and remittance news for those.

Read the three-dot rows first, then apply the so-what line: if you track only two dials, track home-loan rates for the mid-income door and the stock market for luxury. Together they explain most of this cycle, including why luxury and affordable diverged.

c7.story:
Why do the same few listed developers keep taking market share, cycle after cycle? Look at the bottlenecks, because most of them punish the small and reward the large.

The first is approvals. Before a single brick goes in, a project needs environmental clearance, fire safety approval, height clearance from the airport authority if it is near a flight path, municipal building plan approval and more. This can take one to three years. A developer that bought land without approvals has bought dead capital, paying interest while it waits. Large developers have teams that do nothing but manage this queue, and the cash to wait.

The second is land titles. Indian land records are notoriously messy: unclear titles, family disputes, old tenancy claims, farmland that was never properly converted. Clean, litigation-free land is scarce and carries a big premium. A brand that has never had a title dispute is worth real money to buyers.

The third is the one that ends cycles: affordability. City prices have risen much faster than salaries since 2021. At some point the mid-income buyer simply cannot afford the next flat, however low the rate. That is the cyclical bottleneck, and it is biting now.

Approvals and land titles are why scale wins. Affordability is why cycles end.

Then come the rules that cut both ways. RERA's escrow requirement keeps most buyer money inside each project's account, so a developer cannot use one project's cash to fund another, the trick that sank many developers in the last bust. It protects buyers and constrains developers, which is exactly why buyers now prefer developers who can live with it. Stamp duty and GST without input credit raise the cost of buying and push some deals into cash.

The slow one is the stock of stalled projects left by bankrupt rivals: they compete for buyers, but the insolvency process also feeds cheap land to the strong. And the recurring one is the weather and the calendar: monsoon rains and migrant workers heading home for harvest and festivals make quarterly handovers lumpy.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck: its name, why it bites and a severity label. The label tells you how to think about each.

  • Structural: approvals, land titles, and stamp duty and GST. Three permanent features of Indian real estate. They do not change with the cycle; they explain why the industry is consolidating into large, trusted names.
  • Cyclical: the affordability ceiling. The only cyclical row, and the one the so-what line singles out as the one that ends this cycle.
  • Two-sided: RERA's escrow, which locks cash inside each project. It protects buyers and slows weak developers, which is good for the listed names you might own.
  • Slow: bankrupt rivals' stalled projects, a gradual source of competition and of cheap land.
  • Recurring: monsoon and labour, the seasonal reason handovers bunch up in some quarters.

Read the table top to bottom and you can see the thesis of the industry's last five years in it. The structural rows favour scale. The two-sided row favours compliance. The cyclical row is the risk. So the investment question is not whether listed developers will keep gaining share, which the structural rows suggest they will, but whether the market they are gaining share of is about to shrink as affordability bites.

A practical use: when a developer's handovers fall in a quarter, check the recurring row before panicking. When its unsold inventory rises in a city, check the cyclical row and the clock card.

c8.story:
For most of the 2000s, buying an under-construction flat in India was an act of faith. Developers took buyers' money, used some of it to buy land for the next project, and delivered late, or sometimes never. Then, in 2016, Parliament passed the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, and from 2017 the rules of the game changed.

RERA did three big things. Every project had to be registered with the state authority, with its approvals, timelines and plans disclosed. Most of the money collected from buyers had to go into a project-specific escrow account, usable only for that project's land and construction. And developers became accountable for delivery dates, with penalties for delay. The effect was a sorting: small, cash-strapped developers found it much harder to operate, and buyers flocked to large listed names who could live with the rules. RERA is a large part of why the post-2020 boom favoured listed developers so heavily.

RERA did not make property cheaper. It made trust expensive, and the big developers already owned it.

The insolvency code added another twist. Homebuyers were recognised as financial creditors, giving them a seat at the table when a developer went bankrupt, and stalled projects became available for stronger developers to take over and finish.

Then the state-level rules. Stamp duty, charged on every sale, is set state by state and can be a powerful lever: Maharashtra's temporary cut in 2020 pulled forward a wave of sales. Municipal rules on how much can be built on a plot, the floor space index, and Mumbai's society redevelopment rules decide how much new inventory old land can yield.

Above them sit the national dials. RBI and the National Housing Bank set rates and lending limits that decide EMIs. Income-tax rules on home-loan interest and capital gains, including the removal of indexation in 2024, change the after-tax return of buying and selling. And SEBI's REIT and InvIT rules give developers a way to sell finished offices and malls into listed trusts and recycle the cash.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who, what, why you care, and status.

  • Always: five rows. State RERA authorities, stamp duty and registration, GST on under-construction flats, the insolvency code and the environment ministry's clearances. These are the permanent frame of the business, and several of them, RERA and the insolvency code especially, have tilted the field towards large developers.
  • Live: four rows. RBI and the National Housing Bank, the income-tax rules on property, municipal FSI and redevelopment rules, and SEBI's REIT and InvIT rules. These are moving parts that shape demand and capital right now.

Notice there is nothing marked new or coming. This is a mature rulebook: the big changes, RERA and GST, came in 2017, and the industry has spent the years since adapting to them.

Use the why-you-care column to decide who a headline hits. A stamp duty change hits developers in that one state, usually for a quarter or two. An RBI move hits mid-income and affordable developers through EMIs and annuity owners through valuations. A municipal FSI change can unlock land for developers with old plots in that city, which is why Mumbai's redevelopment rules matter so much to Mumbai-focused names. A delayed environmental clearance pushes a specific launch back by quarters.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Five forces asks who keeps the money once it comes in. Run a residential developer and an annuity owner through it and you see why the market pays so much more for a rupee of rent than for a rupee of flat profit.

Start with rivalry. Every Indian city has dozens of developers, listed and unlisted, and in a slow market the unlisted ones discount aggressively to raise cash. A buyer looking at three similar towers in Whitefield can play them against each other. A top mall, by contrast, has few direct rivals in its catchment: Phoenix's malls tend to be the destination, and a rival needs years to assemble land nearby.

Suppliers come next, and here the residential developer has a peculiar problem. The scarce input is land, and landowners know it. In a hot market they demand higher prices or bigger shares in joint developments, eating into the margin of future projects. Construction contractors, by comparison, are plentiful. The annuity owner, which already owns its land, faces little supplier pressure.

Buyers: homebuyers shop around and can simply walk away in a downturn, which is why discounts appear quickly when a cycle turns. A mall or office tenant, once it has fitted out its space, faces high costs to move.

Entrants: in theory anyone with land can become a developer. In practice RERA, funding and approvals now favour scale, which has raised the bar. For malls, land assembly alone is a barrier.

Substitutes are the quiet force. In India renting is cheap relative to buying, so a buyer who balks at the price can rent for years. Resale homes compete with new ones. Offices briefly faced work from home.

A developer has to win every sale again. A landlord wins the tenant once and collects for years.

That one sentence is why the annuity shape on this card is smaller, and why the market rewards it with a steadier valuation.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: residential developers and annuity owners. Look at size first. The residential shape is bigger on every spoke. The annuity shape sits entirely inside it, never crossing.

  • Rivalry is the residential shape's longest spoke, at two and a half, against one and a half for annuity owners. Dozens of developers in every city against a few destination malls.
  • Suppliers show the biggest relative gap: two for residential, one for annuity. That is the landowner, holder of the scarce input, squeezing developers.
  • Buyers and entrants score two against one and a half on both, a moderate gap.
  • Substitutes are the lowest spoke for both, one and a half against one: renting and resale for residential, briefly remote work for offices.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason. The scores are moderate overall, with no three anywhere; this is not a brutal industry, just one where the annuity owner has the steadier seat.

Redraw the shape for the company you own. A luxury developer with land bought decades ago scores lower on suppliers than the average. A regional developer in an oversupplied micro-market scores higher on rivalry. A mall owner with a new rival opening nearby scores higher on rivalry too. The so-what line gives the summary: annuity owners keep the profit through the whole cycle, branded developers with cheap land mainly in the up-cycle.

c10.story:
A developer's quarterly results arrive with two documents: the financial statements and the operational update. Read the second one first. Most of the eight numbers on this card come from it.

Pre-sales value and volume come first, and the split matters as much as the total. If pre-sales value is rising but the area sold is flat or falling, the growth is coming from price, not demand. That is exactly the late-cycle pattern of 2025 and 2026, and it is the single most useful signal on this card.

Collections come next: how much cash actually arrived from buyers. A developer can book impressive pre-sales from a launch, but if collections lag, either the buyers are slow or the bookings were softer than they looked.

Value up, volume down: the market is still paying, but fewer people are buying.

Then the balance-sheet numbers. Net debt to equity tells you whether the developer is borrowing to buy land, the behaviour that killed developers in the last bust. Inventory days tell you how long land and flats sit before turning into cash; a rise with flat pre-sales is a warning that unsold stock is building.

The launch pipeline and land additions are the next two years of sales. A healthy developer launches somewhat more than it sold this year, on land bought at a sensible multiple of the revenue it will generate. Aggressive land buying at high prices, late in a cycle, is a red flag however exciting the press release sounds.

Finally the reported numbers. The EBITDA margin on handovers tells you how profitable projects sold years ago turned out. Rental income and occupancy measure the annuity side. And return on capital asks the hardest question: through a full cycle, did all that land and concrete earn more than it cost?
c10.read:
The table has one row per number: what it tells you, what good looks like and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask each developer. Notice that the first row, pre-sales value and volume, asks two questions at once; read them separately.
  • What good looks like is the benchmark, the only column with figures. Several rows give different benchmarks for residential and annuity businesses, because a mall should have a much higher margin and a lower return on capital than a flat seller.
  • Today's industry median is filled in for the five rows that map to annual filings: net debt, inventory days, EBITDA margin, rental income growth read through revenue growth, and ROCE. Pre-sales, collections and the launch pipeline come from operational updates, so they show a dash; read them from each company's quarterly investor presentation.

A caution specific to this industry: the median includes the road trusts and HUDCO filed here, and it reflects reported numbers, which lag sales by years. So a median EBITDA margin describes projects sold in an earlier phase of the cycle, not today's pricing.

The trick is to compare three things for each company: its own number, the median and the good mark. In a late cycle, the developer to prefer has falling inventory days, little or no net debt, and pre-sales growth that comes from volume as well as price. That is the company the call describes: net cash, land bought cheap.

c11.story:
The earliest warnings about Indian real estate come not from developers' presentations but from the people around them: the registration office, the property consultant, the home-loan desk, the IT company's HR team.

Start with what is happening now. Mumbai's property registrations come out every month from the state's registration data, a live read of transactions in India's largest market. They do not forecast; they confirm.

One quarter ahead sit three signals. Home-loan disbursements and rates: cheaper loans turn into site visits and bookings within a quarter. Unsold inventory reports from property consultants: rising inventory means discounting and weaker pre-sales next. And the stock market: equity gains fund luxury down payments, with a lag of about a quarter.

Two quarters ahead sit the job signals. IT hiring and pay rises turn into home purchases a few quarters later, once the new employee is settled and the raise has landed. Office leasing by global capability centres creates new office jobs, which become housing demand nearby.

The furthest dot, three quarters or more ahead, is land deals. Land bought today is a launch in a year and a margin for years after. When developers rush to buy land at high prices, they are betting the cycle continues, and history says that is often the moment it does not.

Land bought at the top is the slowest-acting poison in real estate. It shows up years later, as margin.

Put the signals together and you get the three-sign rule: unit sales rising, unsold inventory falling, home-loan rates steady or falling. Today only the last is ticking. Unit sales are flat, with value led by price, and unsold inventory is rising in some micro-markets. On the rule's own scale, one of three is the reading at which a downturn begins, which is why the call, while describing the present as a plateau, leans towards annuity owners and net-cash developers with land bought cheap, and away from those that borrowed to buy land at the top.

The chart places each signal along a line by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read its channel.

For this industry the dots spread across the whole line, which is unusual. One sits at the same quarter: city property registrations. Three sit one quarter ahead: home-loan disbursements and rates, consultants' unsold inventory reports and stock-market returns. Two sit two quarters ahead: IT hiring and wage hikes, and GCC office leasing. And one sits on the far right, at three quarters or more: land deal announcements and prices.

Use the chart as a reading order, right to left. The land dot tells you about margins and launches a year or more out. The two-quarter dots tell you about salaried demand. The one-quarter dots tell you about the next pre-sales release. The registration dot confirms what is already happening.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs. Two carry crosses: unit sales rising, noted as flat with value led by price, and unsold inventory falling, noted as rising in some micro-markets. One carries a tick: home-loan rates steady or falling, cut through 2025.

The call box gives the view: a late-cycle plateau, preferring annuity owners and net-cash developers with cheap land over those that borrowed at the top. Its would-change list is your alert list, and it cuts both ways: unit sales turning up with stable prices would restart the cycle, while a sharp market fall or a funding squeeze would deepen the turn.
